Lamb (Doctrine)
LAM
n.
Old English lamb; Hebrew kebes or seh; Greek amnos (a lamb) and arnion (a young lamb—the dominant term in Revelation). One of the most extensive metaphors in Scripture, running from the Passover lamb through the daily continual offering to John the Baptist’s Behold the Lamb of God and Revelation’s the Lamb that was slain.

📖 Biblical Definition

The lamb is one of the most extensive and theologically central metaphors of Scripture, governing the entire sacrificial system of the OT and supremely the person and work of Christ in the NT. The OT lamb-references are pervasive. The Passover lamb (Ex 12), whose blood on the lintels and door-posts caused the destroying angel to pass over the marked households. The daily continual burnt offering (Ex 29:38-42; Num 28:3-4), two lambs of the first year offered every morning and every evening throughout the year. The Sabbath, new moon, and feast-day offerings, which multiplied the lamb-sacrifices on those days. The sin offering and trespass offering for various ceremonial defilements, often involving lambs. Isaiah 53 sets the prophetic-typological substance at its sharpest: he is brought as a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep before her shearers is dumb, so he openeth not his mouth (Isa 53:7). The Suffering Servant is identified as the lamb who bears the iniquity of His people, sustains their punishment, and accomplishes their atonement. The New Testament fulfillment is direct and explicit. John the Baptist, seeing Christ approach, announces: Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world (John 1:29, 36). The identification is theologically definitive: Christ is the Lamb of God, the substantive reality of which the OT lamb-sacrifices were the typological shadow. 1 Peter 1:18-19: redeemed... with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot. Acts 8:32-35: Philip explains Isaiah 53 to the Ethiopian eunuch, preaching Jesus from the place of the scripture which he read (Isa 53:7, the lamb-to-the-slaughter prophecy). Revelation uses the Lamb as Christ’s dominant title throughout the book: the Lamb that was slain (Rev 5:6, 12); the Lamb that was slain from the foundation of the world (Rev 13:8); the marriage of the Lamb (Rev 19:7-9); the Lamb’s book of life (Rev 21:27); the throne of God and of the Lamb (Rev 22:1, 3). The title appears approximately 28 times in Revelation as the dominant Christological designation. The lamb-doctrine therefore organizes one of the most extensive theological structures in Scripture. The OT lambs were the appointed shadows; Christ is the substantive Lamb of God; His sacrifice is the once-for-all atonement that the daily-continual and Passover and sin-offering lambs typologically anticipated; His exaltation as the Lamb that was slain is the perpetual ground of the saints’ worship in heaven; the marriage supper of the Lamb is the consummate eschatological celebration of the redeemed’s union with their Redeemer.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines LAMB as the young of the sheep kind; in scripture, the most extensive sacrificial metaphor (Passover lamb, daily continual offering, sin-offering, Isaiah 53’s Suffering Servant) culminating in Christ as the Lamb of God who taketh away the sin of the world (John 1:29) and the dominant Christological title of Revelation (the Lamb that was slain).

LAMB, n. — 1. The young of the sheep kind. 2. In scripture, an emblem of meekness and innocence; supremely, the title of Christ as the sacrificial substitute for sin (John 1:29; Rev 5:6, 12; 13:8; 22:1).

PASCHAL LAMB — The lamb killed on the Passover, whose blood marked the door-posts and lintels of the Israelites in Egypt; typologically fulfilled in Christ our Passover (1 Cor 5:7).

📖 Key Scripture

John 1:29 — "The next day John seeth Jesus coming unto him, and saith, Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world!"

Isaiah 53:7 — "He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth: he is brought as a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep before her shearers is dumb, so he openeth not his mouth."

Revelation 5:12 — "Saying with a loud voice, Worthy is the Lamb that was slain to receive power, and riches, and wisdom, and strength, and honour, and glory, and blessing."

1 Peter 1:18-19 — "Forasmuch as ye know that ye were not redeemed with corruptible things, as silver and gold, from your vain conversation received by tradition from your fathers; But with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The lamb-doctrine is corrupted, on one side, by the loss of OT-sacrificial typology that has reduced Christ-as-Lamb to a generic title without the substantive substitutionary-atonement weight the OT lambs and Isaiah 53 prefigure—and on the other by the soft-meek-lamb sentimentalization that has lost the warrior-Lamb of Revelation (the Lamb’s wrath, the Lamb who is also the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Lamb who has overcome).

expand to see more

The loss of OT-sacrificial typology has often reduced Christ-as-Lamb to a generic title of gentle Christology without the substantive substitutionary-atonement weight the OT lambs and Isaiah 53 prefigure. The Lamb of God is, in His OT-anchored substance, the substitutionary sacrifice whose blood is the actual ransom for the soul, whose suffering is the actual bearing of the iniquity of His people, whose death is the actual atonement for sin. The Passover lamb’s blood on the lintels, the daily continual burnt offering twice every day, the sin offering and trespass offering for ceremonial defilement, Isaiah 53’s lamb-to-the-slaughter—all these OT typological substances flow into the apostolic identification of Christ as the Lamb of God. To strip the OT-sacrificial substance is to leave Christ-as-Lamb as a soft sentimental title without the substitutionary-atonement weight Scripture uniformly assigns to it. The recovery is the recovery of the typology: Christ is the Lamb because He is the substantive substitutionary sacrifice the OT lambs typologically anticipated, and His blood is the actual ransom His people are redeemed by.

The opposite corruption is the soft-meek-lamb sentimentalization that has, in much contemporary Christianity, lost the warrior-Lamb of Revelation. The Lamb of Revelation is also the Lion of the tribe of Judah (Rev 5:5); the Lamb opens the seals of judgment (Rev 6); the Lamb is the One whose wrath is so terrible that kings of the earth hide in dens and rocks of the mountains and say fall on us, and hide us from the face of him that sitteth on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb: For the great day of his wrath is come; and who shall be able to stand? (Rev 6:16-17). The Lamb is the One who makes war in righteousness against the beast (Rev 17:14, these shall make war with the Lamb, and the Lamb shall overcome them: for he is Lord of lords, and King of kings). The soft-meek-lamb sentimentalization that retains the meek Christology while losing the warrior-Lamb is not the Christ Revelation actually presents. The recovery is the recovery of the full Christological substance: the meek Lamb who as a sheep before her shearers was dumb at the cross is the same Lamb whose wrath is the terror of the kings of the earth at the day of His coming. The Lamb of God is both meek and mighty, substitutionary-sacrifice and conquering-King, the One who is worthy precisely because He was slain and now lives forever as the consummate Lord.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew kebes / seh (lamb); Greek amnos (lamb; John 1:29; Acts 8:32; 1 Pet 1:19) and arnion (young lamb; dominant in Revelation, ~28 uses); the most extensive sacrificial metaphor in Scripture, culminating in Christ as the Lamb of God whose precious blood is the actual ransom (1 Pet 1:18-19) and whose throne is the throne of God and of the Lamb (Rev 22:1).

Hebrew kebes (H3532) — lamb (the regular sacrificial lamb).

Hebrew seh (H7716) — lamb, sheep (especially the Passover lamb of Ex 12).

Greek amnos (G286) — lamb (John 1:29, 36; Acts 8:32; 1 Pet 1:19).

Greek arnion (G721) — little lamb, lamb; the dominant Christological title in Revelation (~28 uses).

Usage

"Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world—John the Baptist’s definitive identification of Christ as the substantive Lamb of God."

"Worthy is the Lamb that was slain—Rev 5:12’s heavenly worship at the throne, the perpetual ground of the saints’ eternal praise."

"Loss of OT-sacrificial typology strips Christ-as-Lamb of substitutionary weight; soft-meek-lamb sentimentalization loses the warrior-Lamb of Revelation; biblical Lamb of God is both meek substitutionary sacrifice and mighty conquering King."
